claims.text: Cr has a high oxygen affinity in CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys.
Cr preferentially oxidizes during high-temperature exposure because formation of chromium oxide is thermodynamically favorable.
Preferential Cr oxidation promotes formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 or Cr-rich mixed-oxide scale.
The Cr-rich oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen penetration.
The barrier action of the Cr-rich scale provides oxidation resistance.
Reducing the Cr concentration compromises the integrity or continuity of the protective oxide scale.
Reducing the Cr concentration leads to increased oxidation rates.
The baseline Cantor alloy is expected to develop and retain a stable, adherent Cr2O3 layer at 1000–1100 °C in air for up to 200 hours.
The baseline alloy is expected to show lower weight gain than the reduced-Cr variant.
The baseline alloy is expected to exhibit slower oxidation kinetics than the reduced-Cr variant.
The proposed comparison holds the oxidation temperature, atmosphere, and exposure duration identical while varying Cr concentration.
Weight gain, scale thickness, scale continuity, phase identity, and oxide chemistry are the proposed response variables.
Comparable protective-scale formation and oxidation resistance in the reduced-Cr and baseline alloys would falsify the claim that preferential Cr oxidation is the primary driver.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys in which selective oxidation predominates under 1000–1100 °C air exposure for up to 200 hours.
